items.title: Alex Kendrick’s Blunt Message to Christians
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Encouraging.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Filmmaker Alex Kendrick is gearing up for a fascinating theatrical expedition as he and his brother, Stephen, prepare to return to their roots in a truly unique way.

In fact, the brothers are set to release, “Flywheel: Ignition of the Soul,” on Oct. 16, a remake of their popular 2003 movie, “Flywheel.”

“‘Flywheel’ was our very first movie shot in standard definition, not even high definition, over 20 years ago,” Alex Kendrick recently told CBN News. “And [I] kind of fell on my face thinking I could make a good feature film, and it turned out to be pretty low production quality.”

In fact, he said, he almost didn’t release the movie as he didn’t realize at the time how difficult filmmaking can be. Ultimately, though, the brothers proceeded — and the rest is history.

“The only thing I did right was beg God to use it,” Kendrick said. “And my brother Stephen helping me and saying, ‘We need to pray Ephesians 3:20 — that God would do exceedingly abundantly more than we could ask or imagine. So that’s the only thing we did right.”

Despite being green filmmakers at the time, the Kendricks were shocked to see how God showed up. “Flywheel” sold 1.3 million DVDs and had a massive response from audiences — much larger than they could have ever imagined.

“People said once they got over the production quality, like 10 minutes into it, then they were moved by the story, and they would come back and say, ‘I saw a version of myself on the screen,'” Kendrick said. “And the the Lord did what only the Lord can do by touching their hearts, and so we’ve always wanted to remake that, and higher quality over the years.”

That idea started coming to fruition two years ago, when the Kendricks were in Brazil releasing, “The Forge,” another faith-based film. The duo took some young Christian filmmakers through a boot camp and, through that experience and through prayer, the idea was birthed to work with teams there to remake, “Flywheel.”

“The Lord opened the door for us to remake, ‘Flywheel,'” he said. “We instantly got the funding, the support, the distribution, so we reshot it in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in Portuguese, and had wonderful cast and crew that love the Lord help us make it, and so it’s made in their culture, their language. They’re so thrilled about it.”

Kendrick said pre-screenings of the film have left audiences crying and cheering. The movie has now been dubbed for Americans audiences into English. Regardless of the language in which the film is viewed, Kendrick believes audiences will love it.

“This movie that talks about lordship and is now modernized [and] is coming out in theaters Oct. 16,” he said. “Can’t wait to see what the Lord does with this one.”

Kendrick believes this movie is releasing at the right cultural moment, with the main character working as a successful used car salesman when he goes through a very dark time in his life. This man realizes he needs more than his own logic to navigate it all, seeking help in marriage, fatherhood — and more. It’s his newfound faith in Jesus that changes everything.

“We do not need more lukewarm Christians,” Kendrick said. “What we need is Christians who are sold out and truly followers of Jesus Christ.”

He continued, “When people see the life of a Christian, what they don’t need to see is half-hearted commitment to our Savior, and half-hearted integrity. They need to see someone who lives for a higher purpose, because we serve an almighty God and that the way we live bears fruit of that relationship.”

Kendrick is hoping — much like the first “Flywheel” — people see themselves on the screen and confront spiritual issues in their own lives.

items.title: PRAY: 24-Year-Old Youth Pastor Dies Running Portland Marathon
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: A youth pastor died after rounding one of the miles of the Portland Marathon on Sunday. Treyton “Trey” Lara, 24, […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A youth pastor died after rounding one of the miles of the Portland Marathon on Sunday.

Treyton “Trey” Lara, 24, reportedly collapsed just before mile 20 of the marathon, right after slowing down briefly to give his wife, Audrey Shin-Lara, a kiss between miles 18 and 19.

“He ran over, was able to give me a kiss, was smiling, and then ran off,” she told local Portland news outlet KGW-TV. “He looked good. And then so I drove off to the finish line, where the rest of our family and friends were going to watch him finish.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Trey Lara (@treytonlara)

Audrey, 24, had been moving with him the entire race. She first stopped to cheer him on at mile 10, then mile 14, then mile 18, and was headed to the end to celebrate all together.

The now-grieving wife said Trey had been training for months and showed no signs of distress of health issues at all, describing running as something her husband did to “relax and release.”

Soon after loading into the car to head to the finish line, Audrey said her mother-in-law called her, telling her Trey had collapsed around mile 20 and that first responders were performing CPR on him. He was transported to a nearby hospital but, by that point, doctors said it was too late.

“We’re all still in a little bit of shock,” said Audrey. “We tried going to bed and we’re like, ‘We’re gonna wake up and it’ll be a really bad dream. And he’ll be right there.'”

While they were married for just under five years, Audrey told reporters they first met one another at 12 years old. She called her late husband “one of one.”

“We met at a summer camp,” she remembered. “He saw me, and I guess he told his friends and even his best friend’s mom, he said, ‘That’s the girl I’m going to marry.’ And I didn’t actually believe it, but now I want to believe it.”

Camp was clearly a major theme in the Laras’ lives.

The couple had just launched a youth summer camp of their own, Camp Genesis, this past summer.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Trey Lara (@treytonlara)

“[I]t was just this dream that he had,” Audrey said of the nascent ministry. “He was the biggest dreamer but it wasn’t just like, ‘I’m going to do this,’ but he’s like, ‘I will do this,’ and we got it done.”

Loved ones set up a GoFundMe campaign to raise money as the family walks through this difficult time. The account describes Trey as a man whose “confidence was unshakable and his faith unwavering.”

“His faith was his defining feature,” it states. “It has spoken the loudest to those who knew him, whether they spent years with him, months with him, or even just a single day. They recognized that Trey’s faith and passion for advancing the Kingdom of God were at the center of his life.”

“He was devoted to his family and friends,” it continues. “He loved his wife, Audrey, from the moment he met her. His sisters, Jaylah and Sylvia, had the best role model in an older brother, and his parents, Omar and Misty, had the most devoted son. The man Trey became directly reflected the values they instilled in him.”

The purpose of the campaign, it notes, is to provide for Audrey’s immediate needs in the wake of her husband’s death.

Please pray for the Laras and all those impacted by this loss.

items.title: It’s Not Just You: Instagram Has Been Pushing Creed’s ‘Higher’ on Everyone’s Stories But Doesn’t Know Why
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: If you posted a photo of your dog, a dinner plate or a caesar salad to your Instagram Story lately and the app suggested Creed’s “Higher” to go with it, you weren’t imagining things. A company spokesperson told CNN the team “looked into this and found that this song is being recommended to mor
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

If you posted a photo of your dog, a dinner plate or a caesar salad to your Instagram Story lately and the app suggested Creed’s “Higher” to go with it, you weren’t imagining things. A company spokesperson told CNN the team “looked into this and found that this song is being recommended to more people than intended.” The company is still investigating, she said, and its engineering team is working on a fix.

Her first response, when she was asked about it, was a little less official: “That song is always recommended to me too!”

Users have been noticing for weeks. “I can’t prove it but pretty sure Creed is paying META to suggest their song ‘Higher’ on all Instagram Stories,” one person wrote on X in August. In September, another posted that they had found out it was happening to other people and said, “I feel like I’m uncovering a big conspiracy.” A third said Instagram “almost had me this time” with a caesar salad.

Instagram is supposed to pick songs the same way it recommends everything else, weighing signals like which songs you have used before and what is in the photo or video you have selected. Nothing about a cat or a plate of pasta should point to a 1999 rock radio staple.

Pamela Ross, a communications specialist, said it happened every time she posted anything to her Story, “like a dinner plate or my cat or whatever.” She told CNN, “I’m not following Creed, I’m not listening to Creed. Like what millennial was in charge of this decision?”

Instagram’s answer is that nobody was. It was a mistake, and it is being fixed.

Creed is not the only song people have been side-eyeing. Some users also flagged Soulja Boy’s “Turn My Swag On” for showing up more often than seemed plausible. Instagram says that one is working as designed: “The Soulja Boy song being recommended is not a bug, and it is actually popular on IG!”

So the Soulja Boy suggestions reflect real demand, and the Creed suggestions were a mistake. If your Story has spent the past few weeks trying to go “Higher,” that was Instagram’s doing, and nothing about your taste put it there.

items.title: Don’t Look Back in Anger: The Power of Forgiveness
items.author: Matthew Malone
items.summary:
Matthew Malone

The story of the Gallagher brothers and the enduring music of Oasis highlight the transformative power of forgiveness and reconciliation.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Matthew Malone

Oasis are undoubtedly one of the biggest bands of the 1990s. With iconic singles like “Wonderwall” and “Don’t Look Back in Anger,” they helped define the Britpop phenomenon and bring it to the international stage. Yet behind the extraordinary success lay a turbulent relationship between the band’s two central figures, brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher. Their relationship was marked by bitter arguments and public feuds, leading to the band’s explosive end in 2009 and its prolonged estrangement that lasted more than a decade. 

Recently, I went to the premiere of the new documentary Don’t Look Back in Anger in which Noel uncharacteristically reflected on his own shortcomings, confessing, “I have a fatal flaw. I can’t forgive people.” I will explore the story of the Gallagher brothers, the enduring music of Oasis, and the transformative power of forgiveness and reconciliation. 

Noel and Liam Gallagher were born in Manchester, UK, to Irish immigrants Peggy and Tommy Gallagher in 1967 and 1972, respectively. Both were baptized at St. Bernard’s Catholic Church in Burnage, Manchester. Tommy was a raging alcoholic and often abusive, with Noel recalling in the documentary Supersonic (2016) that his father had “beat the talent into him.” In 1982, Peggy left her husband, raising the children alone while working several jobs as a housekeeper, nanny, and school cook. 

The brothers developed a reputation for trouble early on, with Noel expelled from school at fifteen. Around this time, he discovered music, particularly the Smiths, whose appearance on Top of the Pops sparked his musical ambitions. He subsequently became a roadie for Madchester band Inspiral Carpets. Liam, however, was more interested in football, and, as the youngest, had been relatively shielded from their father’s abuse. His focus changed following an alleged hammer attack by a student from a rival school. He became obsessed with the Stone Roses and John Lennon. 

Liam joined the band The Rain with schoolmates Paul “Guigsy” McGuigan, Paul “Bonehead” Arthurs, and Tony McCarroll. Liam suggested changing the band’s name to Oasis after noticing it on a tour poster in his brother’s bedroom. Noel attended one of their early performances. Impressed by what he witnessed, he joined in 1991. Noel brought his formidable songwriting and business acumen, complementing Liam’s raw, brash, and arrogant persona. In 1993, the band caught the attention of Creation Records founder Alan McGee following a poorly attended show in Glasgow. McGee signed them on the spot, recalling the following year, “This group, Oasis, are the one recent thing that made me go ‘I still believe in rock ’n’ roll.’ I saw them last year, and it was a complete fluke. . . . Seeing them is what seeing the Stones must have been like in the early days. Brutal, exciting, arrogant.” 

Oasis released Definitely Maybe in 1994, which became the fastest selling debut album in British history at the time. Featuring “Supersonic” and “Live Forever,” the album heralded the band as the kings of Britpop. “Live Forever,” written partially as a tribute to their mother, Peggy, was Noel’s response to the nihilism of American grunge. Reflecting on its inspiration, he recalled, “I remember Nirvana had a tune called ‘I Hate Myself and Want to Die’ and I was like, I’m not —— having that. . . . I can’t have people coming over here on smack, —— saying that they hate themselves and they wanna die. That’s —— rubbish. Kids don’t need to be hearing that nonsense.” 

The following year, Oasis released (What’s The Story) Morning Glory?, featuring the now iconic “Wonderwall” and “Don’t Look Back in Anger.” The album sold more than 300,000 copies in its first week in Britain and propelled the band to international fame, achieving multi-platinum status in the US. In 1996, Neil Strauss wrote in The New York Times, “In Britain the band reigns unchallenged as the most popular act since the Beatles. There is an Oasis CD in roughly one of every three homes there; last month, the band drew 250,000 people to Knebworth, north of London, for the biggest outdoor concerts in the country’s history.” 

Oasis had become a cultural phenomenon. Yet their Beatles-like success stood in stark contrast to the increasingly petulant relationship between the Gallagher brothers. Their volatile arguments—fueled by alcohol, drug use, and resentment—repeatedly tested the band’s resolve to continue. During the Morning Glory recording sessions, one notorious confrontation saw Noel strike a heavily intoxicated Liam with a cricket bat. The band came to an end in 2009, with Noel announcing his departure on the band’s website, “It’s with some sadness and great relief to tell you that I quit Oasis tonight. People will write and say what they like but I simply could not go on working with Liam a day longer.” 

In the following years, Noel and Liam pursued solo careers while their resentment and estrangement deepened. Their animosity played out publicly in a succession of witty insults. Noel once quipped, “I liked my mum until she gave birth to Liam,” and “I don’t listen to Liam’s albums because I can’t stand his voice. . . . I think it’s unsophisticated music. For unsophisticated people. Made by an unsophisticated man.” Liam was equally scathing, describing Noel as “the angriest man you’ll ever meet” and likening him to “a man with a fork in a world of soup.” Despite constant speculation about a reunion, Noel was adamant, “There will never be a reunion with my brother Liam.”

The Gallagher brothers’ story echoes various famous sibling conflicts in the Bible: Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, and perhaps most notably, the brothers in Christ’s parable of the prodigal son. Noel was the dutiful brother, writing the majority of Oasis’s songs and often holding the band together, while Liam played the prodigal, bringing his volatile energy, unpredictability, and appetite for sensational headlines. For more than fifteen years, their estrangement continued, leaving the media, fans, bandmates, and family wondering whether they would ever speak again. 

It’s uncertain what prompted it, but on August 27, 2024, Oasis announced their reunion: “The guns have fallen silent. The stars have aligned. The great wait is over. Come see. It will not be televised.” 

The new documentary Don’t Look Back in Anger, conceived by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight and directed by Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern, offers an intimate glimpse of the brothers’ unspoken reconciliation. 

The film opens with a montage of fifteen years of insults and speculation before bringing the audience into an Oasis rehearsal room. Noel deftly directs the band through their old songs, eventually asking, “So when is Liam coming in?” The answer: “Tomorrow.” When Liam arrives, the brothers briefly acknowledge each other and get down to the business of rehearsal. Knight reflects, 

In that huge moment when Liam arrives on the first day for the first time the brothers are going to perform together for over fifteen years, there isn’t a high-five, a hug, or even a word between them. . . . And the relationship builds as they’re doing the actual work. And that’s what I love about it and why I think people get it and feel the emotion—because you’re feeling the emotion they’re not expressing.

The documentary frames this understated reconciliation through a homily on forgiveness delivered by Fr. Luke Bradbury, a priest at St. Bernard’s Catholic Church in Burnage where the Gallagher brothers were baptized and their mother Peggy remains a devoted parishioner. Coincidentally, on the only day the filmmakers were able to film at the church, Fr. Bradbury was preaching on Matt 18:21–35. He beautifully connects the Catholic call to forgiveness with the reunion shows taking place in Cardiff, presenting Noel and Liam’s reconciliation as a source of inspiration for anyone carrying the pain of a broken or wounded relationship. 

The homily begins with Peter asking Jesus, “Lord, if another member of the church sins against me, how often should I forgive? As many as seven times?” Jesus replies, “Not seven times, but, I tell you, seventy-seven times.” Over a montage of Oasis fans congregating at the show, Fr. Bradbury continues,  

Forgiveness is hard; it costs us something. But if we refuse to forgive, we imprison ourselves, we carry bitterness, anger, and shame. Forgiveness doesn’t necessarily mean forgetting what happened, it means deciding not to carry it with you anymore. It means looking forward, not back. So let me ask you today: Who do you need to forgive? A friend? A sibling? A parent? Maybe even yourself?

It’s poignant that Fr. Bradbury makes the crucial distinction that forgiveness is not the same as forgetting. This is one of the most important lessons in Noel and Liam’s very human story. Their reunion doesn’t erase fifteen years of resentment. Forgiveness is framed as an act of liberation. This is perhaps a more subtle point of Christ’s teaching: We are called to forgive in light of pain, not because it’s no longer present.

This calls to mind Christ on the cross. He innocently endured the greatest suffering that humanity can inflict upon a person, yet from the cross he cries out, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” Forgiveness does not deny the reality of suffering, instead it is the call to affirm love in spite of suffering and injustice. 

The Catholic understanding of reconciliation goes much deeper than simply making peace. It is the restoration of communion—with God and with others. In the sacrament of reconciliation, we acknowledge our sins, seek forgiveness, and are restored to communion, allowing us to return to the Eucharist and participate in the sacramental life of the Church. Reconciliation opens the door to what St. Paul called the theological virtues: “Faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love.” And as Christ perfectly demonstrated through his sacrifice on the cross, love is the ultimate destination. 

Fr. Bradbury’s homily is a beautiful, heart-rending, and unifying moment in musical documentary history. It reminds us that reconciliation must ultimately be lived through action, not just in words—or even songs. Perhaps no Oasis song could provide a more fitting soundtrack to the brother’s reunion than “Don’t Look Back in Anger,” also the documentary’s title. The song was written by Noel in 1995 and became their most iconic song. It took on a greater significance after the Manchester Arena bombing in 2017, when it became a rallying cry of solidarity and defiance. Only three days after the terrorist attack, a huge crowd gathered in St. Ann’s Square and spontaneously broke into a rendition of the song following a minute’s silence for the twenty-two victims. The moment transformed a pop song into an anthem of healing and forgiveness. It is almost as if, after more than a decade of conflict and insults, the Gallagher brothers could finally begin to live up to the words of their own anthem. 

The song and the Gallagher reunion suggest the power of music and celebrity to bring generations together in something approaching a spiritual experience of unity. Throughout the documentary, fans can be seen crying and even praying at Oasis shows, and describing how Oasis’s music gave them hope during difficult times in their own lives, while others recount how the brothers’ reunion inspired them to reconnect with friends and family. If Liam and Noel can forgive each other, so can we. The reconciliation has become more than the reunion of a ’90s rock ’n’ roll band—for people the world over, it became a catalyst for hope and inspiration amidst a world marred by sin, conflict, and division. 

As a lifelong Oasis fan, I know that for me personally, seeing the Gallagher brothers live again on the recent tour was a beautiful and unifying experience. I went with my father and two of my three younger brothers. It was an emotional moment, especially given the fact that I had experienced periods of estrangement within my own family. When Noel walked up to the microphone and the piano intro began, I remember putting my arms around my father and brothers and all of us screaming at the top of our lungs: 

Don’t look back in anger,
I heard you say . . .

items.title: Friday, October 9, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, we learn of a person possessed by a demon.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Galatians 3:7-14

So, you see, those who believe are the descendants of Abraham. And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, declared the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “All the Gentiles shall be blessed in you.” For this reason, those who believe are blessed with Abraham who believed.

For all who rely on the works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who does not observe and obey all the things written in the book of the law.” Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law; for “The one who is righteous will live by faith.” But the law does not rest on faith; on the contrary, “Whoever does the works of the law will live by them.” Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree”— in order that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

Psalm
Psalm 111:1b-2, 3-4, 5-6

Praise the Lord!
I will give thanks to the Lord with my whole heart,
    in the company of the upright, in the congregation.
Great are the works of the Lord,
    studied by all who delight in them.
Full of honor and majesty is his work,
    and his righteousness endures forever.
He has gained renown by his wonderful deeds;
    the Lord is gracious and merciful.
He provides food for those who fear him;
    he is ever mindful of his covenant.
He has shown his people the power of his works,
    in giving them the heritage of the nations.

Gospel Reading
Luke 11:15-26

But some of them said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons.” Others, to test him, kept demanding from him a sign from heaven. But he knew what they were thinking and said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself becomes a desert, and house falls on house. If Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? —for you say that I cast out the demons by Beelzebul. Now if I cast out the demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your exorcists cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out the demons, then the kingdom of God has come to you. When a strong man, fully armed, guards his castle, his property is safe. But when one stronger than he attacks him and overpowers him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his plunder. Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.

“When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it wanders through waterless regions looking for a resting place, but not finding any, it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ When it comes, it finds it swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and live there; and the last state of that person is worse than the first.”

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, we learn of a person possessed by a demon. Jesus meets the man and drives out the demon but then is immediately accused of being in league with Satan. Some of the witnesses say, “By the power of Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he drives out demons.”

Jesus’s response is wonderful in its logic and laconicism: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste and house will fall against house. And if Satan is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand?”

The demonic power is always one of scattering. It breaks up communion. But Jesus, as always, is the voice of communio, of one bringing things back together.

Think back to Jesus’s feeding of the five thousand. Facing a large, hungry crowd, his disciples beg him to “dismiss the crowds so that they can go to the villages and buy food for themselves.” But Jesus answers, “There is no need for them to go away; give them some food yourselves.” 

Whatever drives the Church apart is an echo of this “dismiss the crowds” impulse and a reminder of the demonic tendency to divide. In times of trial and threat, this is a very common instinct. We blame, attack, break up, and disperse. But Jesus is right: “There is no need for them to go away.”
